system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-08-10 12:47:00 to 2179-08-11 14:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and multiple comorbidities was admitted with a four-day history of cough and pleuritic chest pain, along with new bilateral leg pain and hematuria. He had undergone dialysis earlier on the day of admission but remained symptomatic. Initial labs revealed severe hyperkalemia (K 8.3), which was treated and resolved. Chest imaging showed chronic interstitial changes without pneumonia or acute findings. He was diagnosed with bronchitis and treated with a five-day course of azithromycin. His respiratory symptoms improved, and he tolerated another dialysis session during the stay. Trace hematuria persisted without signs of infection. He remained stable, was discharged home on his baseline medications plus a short course of antibiotics, and advised to resume outpatient dialysis and follow up with his nephrologist.
problems: Bronchitis, not specified as acute or chronic
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits

conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you had chest pain during dialysis today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. It came on suddenly—sharp pain right here over my left chest. Lasted about five minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did it go anywhere else? Like your arm or neck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it goes up to my right neck. I took a nitroglycerin tablet and it went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’ve had something like this before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three days ago. Same kind of pain, same spot. Also went away with nitro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Was it brought on by activity or was it at rest?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both times, I was just sitting. No exertion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any shortness of breath, nausea, or sweating with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the pain. I’ve had cardiac pain before, and this feels very similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll take this very seriously. You’re also mentioning you’ve had diarrhea for a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about five days now. Three loose stools a day, but no blood, no fever, no belly pain. I’m still eating normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear. We’ll monitor that, but it doesn’t seem severe. Let me go over your history quickly—you have coronary artery disease, had stents placed, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two drug-eluting stents in the right coronary artery. They wanted me to have bypass surgery years ago, but I declined.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And you’re on dialysis three times a week—Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I did dialysis earlier today before the chest pain started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked your EKG. It shows no acute changes—no heart attack pattern. Your rhythm is normal, though you do have some old changes from prior heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on the EKG and your first troponin level—which measures heart muscle damage—it’s not showing that. But we’ll check it again over the next few hours to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat troponins came back negative—three times now. That’s reassuring. No sign of heart muscle damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what was the chest pain from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given how it felt like your prior angina, responded to nitroglycerin, and occurred at rest, we believe it was angina—your heart not getting enough oxygen for a short time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But no blockage this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule out a temporary spasm or a partial blockage that didn’t cause permanent damage. But you’re stable now, no pain, and your labs are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start you on a new medication called Imdur—a long-acting nitrate. It helps prevent angina episodes by keeping your heart vessels open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same as the nitro I take under my tongue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, but Imdur works all day. The nitro under your tongue is for quick relief when pain happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I still go to dialysis tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for tomorrow, but we’ll coordinate with nephrology. Your kidney function is stable, and your labs show no urgent need for dialysis today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no episodes since admission, and you’re tolerating food and fluids. We don’t see signs of infection. Likely a mild viral or dietary issue. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without any chest pain. Your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain at all. I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll go home with the Imdur prescription and continue all your usual heart and dialysis meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to follow up with cardiology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very important. You’ll have an appointment with the cardiology nurse practitioner soon to review this episode and your overall heart health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should resume your regular schedule—next session is Wednesday. Call your dialysis center to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get chest pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—rest and take one nitroglycerin tablet. If it doesn’t go away in five minutes, take another. If it persists after three doses, call 911.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—still no chest pain or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember: take Imdur daily, continue all your other meds, and keep that cardiology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis and a history of coronary artery disease presented with acute chest pain that occurred during dialysis and recurred at rest, relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin. The pain was consistent with angina, though serial troponins were negative and EKG showed no acute changes. He also reported a five-day history of non-bloody, non-febrile diarrhea, which resolved during the admission. He remained stable without further episodes of chest pain, was started on isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) for angina prophylaxis, and continued all baseline medications. He was discharged home with instructions to follow up in cardiology and resume regular dialysis, with no complications during the hospital stay.
problems: Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
